route: The round count of best-response restart and bidirectional improvement: geometric decay of the maximal gap, or a family that switches one vertex many times
headline: A new proved bound R <= m+(m+1)B forces BOTH BSI tracks to be long; a self-dual family SD(K) switches one vertex K times (previous record 4); a readout family RD(n) makes R_BR n rounds and BSI 2n rounds where all-switches takes 1, refuting the standing belief that best-response restart is never slower; both local rate claims about M are refuted by 2^{-Theta(N)} instances.

results.name: rbr:lem-greedy + rbr:thm-track
results.statement: Call v in Vmax U-greedy at sigma if U(sigma(v)) >= U(sigma-bar(v)), and let Phi be the count of U-greedy Max vertices. One round of the STRICT variant of def:bsi has Phi(sigma',U) = Phi(sigma,U) + |C_max| and Phi(sigma',U') >= Phi(sigma',U) - D, where D counts Max vertices un-greedied by the U-update, D <= m, and D = 0 when C_min is empty. Hence, with A = #rounds with C_max nonempty and B = #rounds with C_min nonempty, sum_t |C_max,t| <= m + mB, A <= m(1+B), B <= k(1+A), and R <= m+(m+1)B, R <= k+(k+1)A. Since val^tau strictly decreases at every round with C_min nonempty, B <= 2^k - 1 and dually A <= 2^m - 1, so R = O(N 2^{min(m,k)}) -- BSI is polynomial whenever min(|Vmax|,|Vmin|) = O(log N). Conversely a superpolynomial run forces B >= (R-m)/(m+1) AND A >= (R-k)/(k+1): both tracks must be superpolynomially long improving runs.
results.argument: Switching a strictly vetoed v makes it U-greedy and it was not before; unswitched vertices keep their status; U changes only when C_min is nonempty. Telescoping Phi over the run with 0 <= Phi <= m gives the first display. R <= A+B because every productive round moves at least one track. B <= 2^k-1 because val^tau strictly decreases along the Min track so no Min strategy recurs.
results.verification: Proof from lem:switch, lem:duality, thm:contraction only. Machine-checked: 3000 runs of both variants on random two-player stopping games with 5..13 non-sinks, exact arithmetic (t8_greedy.py); 0 violations of A <= m+D, B <= k+D', R <= m+(m+1)B, R <= k+(k+1)A. Also 0 violations in the 19600-run sweep of t3_rbr.py. Tight up to 1 on SD(K).

results.name: rbr:prop-sd  (the self-dual leapfrog SD(K))
results.statement: For every K there is an acyclic (hence stopping) SSG SD(K) on N = K^2+5K+10 vertices with |Vmax| = |Vmin| = K+1, self-dual in the sense of bsr:prop-selfdual, on which BSI, strict BSI, the one-sided self-dual rule MR, R_BR and all-switches all take exactly K rounds from the mirrored start, C_max = {x_{t+1}, v} and C_min = {u_{t+1}, v'} at round t, so the Max vertex v and the Min vertex v' are each switched K times. M takes the K+1 values 2^{-1},...,2^{-K},0.
results.argument: A Max cascade x_j -> (x_{j-1}, k_j) with k_j of value 1-2^{-j} fires one vertex per round; its phi-mirror u_j -> (u_{j-1}, h_j) with h_j = 2^{-j} does the same on the Min side. Because the game is self-dual and the start mirrored, U = 1 - L o phi, and since phi(p) = q at the observer v the veto reads U(q)-U(p) = L(q)-L(p): the guide and the value AGREE at v, so the veto never blocks. Min-optimal play forces L(u_j) = 0 and Max-free play forces U(x_j) = 1, so L(p)-L(q) = sum_j gamma_j L_t(x_j) + Delta; the weights gamma_j = (-1)^{j+1} 2^{j+1} eta with eta = 2^{-(K+2)} telescope this to (-1)^{t+1} eta for t < K and (-1)^K eta at t = K, so v is switchable and endorsed at every one of the K rounds and not at the last.
results.verification: Exact rational arithmetic, K = 2..20 (t2_family.py, t12_final.py): stopping by lem:trapchar, phi an involution with kinds swapped and successors corresponding, mirrored start, the identity U = 1 - L o phi asserted at EVERY round, round count K, switch multiset (v and v' K times, every x_j and u_j once), level sequence, bracket val_sigma <= w* <= val^tau at every round, and halting at val_sigma = val^tau = w* (w* certified as an exact fixed point of T). Fresh larger sizes K = 6,10,14,16 re-run independently.

results.name: rbr:thm-readout  (the readout cascade RD(n))
results.statement: For every n there is an acyclic stopping SSG RD(n) on N = 9n vertices with |Vmax| = |Vmin| = n on which (a) all-switches halts after at most 1 round from EVERY Max strategy; (b) R_BR of prop:bsi-br takes exactly n rounds from sigma_0, in both veto variants and for every choice of best response, switching the single vertex v_{t+1} at round t; (c) BSI from (sigma_0,tau_0) takes exactly 2n rounds, alternating C_max = {v_{t+1}}, C_min = empty and C_max = empty, C_min = {u_{t+1}}, in both variants. Every controlled vertex switches once. Hence the ratio (rounds of R_BR or of BSI)/(rounds of all-switches) is Theta(N) and unbounded.
results.argument: With f(x) = x/2 + 1/4 (fixed point 1/2), theta_j = 1/2 - 4^{-j} and B_j = 1/2 + 4^{-j} satisfy f(theta_j) < theta_{j+1} < B_{j+1} < f(B_j). Put v_j -> (a_j, b_j) with b_j the constant B_j and a_j = avg(u_{j-1}, H) so val(a_j) = f(val(u_{j-1})), and u_j -> (v_j, Theta_j) with Theta_j the constant theta_j. Then L_t(v_j) = B_j and L_t(u_j) = theta_j for j <= t and L_t(v_j) < theta_j for j > t, so every v_j with j > t is strictly switchable and Min's UNIQUE best response tau_t READS OFF which Max vertices have switched. Consequently U_t(a_{t+1}) = f(theta_t) < B_{t+1} endorses v_{t+1} while U_t(a_j) = f^{j-t-1}(B_{t+1}) > B_j vetoes every later one; the two chains separate because f is increasing and the two inequalities above hold. All-switches, seeing only L, switches all of S_sigma = {v_j : sigma(v_j) = a_j} at once and lands at the optimum.
results.verification: Exact rational arithmetic, n = 2..20 (t9_rd.py, t10_rdtrace.py, t13_starts.py, t12_final.py, t14_table.py): stopping, all-switches = 1, R_BR = n (both variants), BSI = 2n (both variants), the full switched-set trace, bracket at every round, halt at w*. Worst case over all 2^n Max starts = n verified for n <= 4; over every choice of best response at every round for n <= 4; over all 4^n pair starts = 2n for n <= 3. Independently, a random search over 19600 (game,start) pairs found 11-vertex and 12-vertex instances with the same phenomenon (rbr:prop-small), and the value engine was cross-checked against the componentwise extremum over all positional counter-strategies.

results.name: rbr:prop-gain
results.statement: REFUTED: 'within each level the switched Z-vertex's gain is at least a constant fraction of M'. On GAIN(s) (s+5 vertices, one Max z, one Min u, avg H, r_1..r_s with H -> (t0,t1), u -> (t0,H), r_1 -> (u,H), r_i -> (u,r_{i-1}), z -> (t0,r_s)) at sigma(z) = t0, tau(u) = H one has M = max(U-L) = 1/2, z in Z = argmax(U-L), z in C_max in both variants, and the L-gain of the switch is exactly 2^{-s-1} = M*2^{-(N-5)}.
results.argument: L(u) = 0 and L(r_i) = 2^{-i-1} (Min optimal sends u to t0); U(u) = U(r_i) = 1/2 (tau frozen at H). So U(z) - L(z) = 1/2 = M and the gain L(r_s) - L(t0) = 2^{-s-1}. The general identity is M = gain + (U(q)-L(q)) at a switched z in Z with target q, so the gain is small exactly when the target is itself of almost maximal deficit; the chain r_1..r_s drives the deficit of the target to M geometrically.
results.verification: Exact, s = 1,2,4,8,12,16,20,24,30,40 (t4_rate.py and a direct re-run): gain/M = 2^{-s} in every case, z in Z in every case, stopping in every case.

results.name: rbr:prop-slowlevel
results.statement: REFUTED: 'M is halved (or falls by a constant factor) every level, or every O(1) rounds'. SL(K) is a self-dual stopping SSG on N = 6K+4 vertices (mirrored cascades u_i -> (u_{i-1}, e_i), x_i -> (x_{i-1}, f_i) with val(e_i) = 1/2 + 2^{-i-1}) on which BSI takes K rounds, one Min and one Max switch per round, and M_t = 1/2 + 2^{-t-2} for t < K, M_K = 0. So M stays above 1/2 for all K = Theta(N) rounds and its relative drop at round t is 2^{-t-3}/(1/2 + 2^{-t-2}) = 2^{-Theta(N)} at the late rounds.
results.argument: c_i = 1/2 + 2^{-i-1} is strictly decreasing and stays above 1/2, so only u_1 is in S^tau initially and the cascade fires one vertex per round; the deficit at u_i is c_i before its round and 0 after, every average vertex has L = U, and the Max side is the phi-image, so M_t = max_{i>t} c_i = c_{t+1}.
results.verification: Exact, K = 2,3,4,6,8,10,12,16 (t4_rate.py, t14_table.py): round count K, the full level sequence, the relative drops, self-duality and mirrored start, halt at w*.

results.name: rbr:lem-vacuous  (mirror-paired self-dual games)
results.statement: Call a self-dual stopping SSG MIRROR-PAIRED if the involution phi exchanges the two successors of every controlled vertex, phi(v^(0)) = v^(1). Then from a mirrored pair state C_max = S_sigma and C_min = phi(S_sigma) in BOTH variants, the next pair state is again mirrored, and BSI, strict BSI and the one-sided rule MR of bsr:prop-selfdual all run EXACTLY all-switches on the Max cube. Hence a polynomial round bound for BSI entails one for all-switches on this class.
results.argument: bsr:prop-selfdual gives U = 1 - L o phi. At v in Vmax with p = sigma(v), q = sigma-bar(v), mirror-pairing gives phi(p) = q and phi(q) = p, so U(q) - U(p) = (1 - L(p)) - (1 - L(q)) = L(q) - L(p). Therefore v in S_sigma iff U(q) > U(p), which is the strict veto and a fortiori the veto.
results.verification: Proof only from bsr:prop-selfdual. The class's harmonic normal form (rows (A_i,B_i,c_i) with q_i forced to be (B_i,A_i,1-|A_i|-|B_i|-c_i) and L(v_i') = min(L(p_i),L(q_i))) was implemented exactly (psd.py) and searched (psdfast.py + search_psd.py); every reported winner re-verified exactly after dyadic rounding.

results.name: rbr:lem-constant
results.statement: If v in Vmax has sigma(v) = c with val_sigma(c) = val^tau(c) (e.g. c is an average gadget all of whose paths end in sinks) and v is in S_sigma, then v is in C_max, in both variants of def:bsi and in R_BR. Dually at Vmin. Hence at a controlled vertex one of whose two options is a constant gadget, only the switch TOWARDS the constant is ever vetoed.
results.argument: With p = sigma-bar(v): U(p) >= L(p) > L(c) = U(c) by cor:comparison and v in S_sigma, so the veto U(p) >= U(c) holds, and strictly.
results.verification: Exact check on 364 occurrences of the hypothesis drawn from random stopping games (t16_const.py), 0 violations for both the >= and the > form. Consequence recorded in the GAP: the RESET direction of a would-be binary counter is never vetoed; only the SET direction needs the readout machinery.

gap: There is a family of stopping SSGs on N = n^{O(1)} vertices, carrying Max vertices v_1,...,v_n with v_j -> (a_j, b_j) where b_j is a constant gadget, and Min vertices u_1,...,u_n with u_j -> (v_j, Theta_j), in which Theta_j is driven by v_1,...,v_{j-1} rather than being constant, and along the run of def:bsi the two nondecreasing quantities val_sigma(v_j) and val_sigma(Theta_j) cross 2^{n-j} times.
next_steps: (1) Attack the GAP directly. Two directional facts now localise the difficulty. By rbr:lem-constant the RESET b_j -> a_j of such a counter is never vetoed (U(a_j) >= L(a_j) > B_j = U(b_j) automatically), so only the SET a_j -> b_j needs endorsement machinery, and RD(n) already supplies that. A crossing of val_sigma(v_j) by val_sigma(Theta_j) is exactly the leapfrog of SD(K), which costs one driver switch each. So no local, order-theoretic or monotonicity obstruction found in this round blocks the counter; what is missing is a SCHEDULE in which the drivers of the leapfrog at u_j are the recurring lower bits rather than fresh vertices. The concrete next construction is to graft SD(K)'s observer (which switches at every round) onto RD(n)'s cascade (which forces one switch per round) and then make Theta_j read the lower bits. (2) rbr:thm-track says both tracks must be superpolynomially long, so any attempt must be genuinely two-player and tightly interleaved; RD(n) already alternates Max and Min rounds strictly, which is the right shape. Do this by hand, not by search -- the search reached only m rounds at m <= 4, and prop:auso-size says no census can decide realisability. \subsection{The round count of bidirectional improvement and of
best-response restart}\label{rbr:sec}

Throughout $G$ is a stopping SSG, $m:=|\Vmax|$, $k:=|\Vmin|$,
$(\sigma,\tau)$ a pair state, $L:=\val_\sigma$, $U:=\val^\tau$ and
$C_{\max},C_{\min}$ as in \Cref{def:bsi}.  A round is \emph{productive} if
$C_{\max}\cup C_{\min}\ne\emptyset$; by \Cref{thm:bsi-nostall} every
non-final round is productive.

\subsubsection{A second potential: the opponent-greedy count}

\Cref{cor:bsi-levels} measures a BSI run by $(M,|Z|)$.  The following
measures it instead by how many Max vertices agree with the \emph{guide}
$U$, and it is what makes \Cref{prop:bsi-oneplayer} work; the point is that
it survives into two-player games, at the price of a term counting the
times the guide reverses.

\begin{definition}[Guide-greedy count]\label{rbr:def-greedy}
Call $v\in\Vmax$ \emph{$U$-greedy at $\sigma$} if
$U(\sigma(v))\ge U(\bar\sigma(v))$, and put
$\Phi(\sigma,U):=\#\{v\in\Vmax: v\ \text{is $U$-greedy at }\sigma\}$.
Dually $u\in\Vmin$ is \emph{$L$-greedy at $\tau$} if
$L(\tau(u))\le L(\bar\tau(u))$, with count $\Psi(\tau,L)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[One round of the strict rule]\label{rbr:lem-greedy}
Let $(\sigma',\tau')=(\sigma[C_{\max}],\tau[C_{\min}])$ be one round of the
\emph{strict} variant of \Cref{def:bsi}, $L'=\val_{\sigma'}$,
$U'=\val^{\tau'}$.  Then
\[
  \Phi(\sigma',U)=\Phi(\sigma,U)+|C_{\max}|,\qquad
  \Phi(\sigma',U')\ \ge\ \Phi(\sigma',U)-D,
\]
where $D:=\#\{v\in\Vmax:\ v\ \text{is $U$-greedy at }\sigma'\ \text{but not
$U'$-greedy at }\sigma'\}$ satisfies $D\le m$ and $D=0$ whenever
$C_{\min}=\emptyset$.  Dually for $\Psi$.  For the veto variant of
\Cref{def:bsi} the first equality becomes
$\Phi(\sigma',U)=\Phi(\sigma,U)+|C^{>}_{\max}|$, where
$C^{>}_{\max}:=\{v\in C_{\max}: U(\bar\sigma(v))>U(\sigma(v))\}$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
If $v\notin C_{\max}$ then $\sigma'(v)=\sigma(v)$ and its $U$-greediness is
unchanged.  If $v\in C_{\max}$ in the strict variant then
$U(\bar\sigma(v))>U(\sigma(v))$, so $v$ is not $U$-greedy at $\sigma$, while
$\sigma'(v)=\bar\sigma(v)$ makes $U(\sigma'(v))>U(\bar{\sigma'}(v))$, so $v$
is $U$-greedy at $\sigma'$: each such $v$ contributes exactly $+1$.  In the
veto variant a $v$ with $U(\bar\sigma(v))=U(\sigma(v))$ is $U$-greedy before
and after and contributes $0$, whence the last sentence.  The second
inequality is the definition of $D$, and $D=0$ when $U'=U$; and
$U'=\val^{\tau'}$ depends only on $\tau'$, which equals $\tau$ when
$C_{\min}=\emptyset$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Both tracks must be long]\label{rbr:thm-track}
Let a run of the strict variant of \Cref{def:bsi} on a stopping $G$ have $R$
productive rounds, and let
$A:=\#\{t:C_{\max,t}\ne\emptyset\}$, $B:=\#\{t:C_{\min,t}\ne\emptyset\}$.
Then
\[
  \sum_t|C_{\max,t}|\ \le\ m+\sum_tD_t\ \le\ m+mB,\qquad
  A\le m(1+B),\qquad B\le k(1+A),
\]
and therefore
\[
  R\ \le\ m+(m+1)B\qquad\text{and}\qquad R\ \le\ k+(k+1)A .
\]
Since every round with $C_{\min}\ne\emptyset$ strictly decreases $\val^\tau$
at some vertex (\Cref{lem:switch} in $\bar G$ and \Cref{lem:duality}), the
Min strategies occurring at such rounds are pairwise distinct, so
$B\le2^{k}-1$; dually $A\le2^{m}-1$.  Hence
\[
  R\ \le\ \min\bigl\{\,m+(m+1)(2^{k}-1),\ \ k+(k+1)(2^{m}-1)\,\bigr\}
      \ =\ O\bigl(N\,2^{\min(m,k)}\bigr).
\]
In particular BSI halts in polynomially many rounds on every stopping game
with $\min(|\Vmax|,|\Vmin|)=O(\log N)$; and a run of superpolynomial length
forces $B\ge(R-m)/(m+1)$ and $A\ge(R-k)/(k+1)$, so \emph{both} tracks must
be superpolynomially long improving runs.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Write $\Phi_t:=\Phi(\sigma_t,U_t)$.  \Cref{rbr:lem-greedy} gives
$\Phi_{t+1}\ge\Phi_t+|C_{\max,t}|-D_t$; summing over $t<R$ and using
$0\le\Phi_t\le m$ yields $\sum_t|C_{\max,t}|\le m+\sum_tD_t$.  Each $D_t$ is
at most $m$ and vanishes unless $C_{\min,t}\ne\emptyset$, so
$\sum_tD_t\le mB$; and $A\le\sum_t|C_{\max,t}|$.  The dual statement is
\Cref{rbr:lem-greedy} for $\Psi$ read in $\bar G$.  Every productive round
has $C_{\max}\ne\emptyset$ or $C_{\min}\ne\emptyset$, so $R\le A+B$, and
substituting $A\le m(1+B)$ gives $R\le m+(m+1)B$.  Finally $B\le2^{k}-1$
because $\val^{\tau}$ is strictly decreasing along the Min track, so no Min
strategy recurs.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}\label{rbr:rem-track}
\Cref{rbr:thm-track} is the first bound for \Cref{def:bsi} that does not go
through the value grid: \Cref{cor:bsi-correct} gives $2N4^{a}$, and $a$ can
be $\Theta(N)$ while $\min(m,k)$ is $O(1)$.  Its content is the second
sentence of the display: the two tracks bound one another, so a
superpolynomial family cannot be built by making one player work while the
other idles --- exactly the failure mode of the disjoint union
$L_n\sqcup\bar L_n$ noted in \Cref{rem:bsi-gap}.  For the veto variant the
same proof bounds only the rounds at which some \emph{strictly} vetoed Max
vertex is switched; the remaining rounds switch only $U$-tied Max vertices
and $L$-tied Min ones, and on the tied set the veto is vacuous, so there
\Cref{def:bsi} \emph{is} all-switches.  The displayed bounds were never
violated in $3000$ runs of both variants on random two-player stopping
games with up to $13$ non-sinks.
\end{remark}

\subsubsection{The leapfrog is cheap: one vertex switched $K$ times}

\Cref{prop:bsi-twice} switches a vertex twice; the round-$14$ instance
$Q_{16}$ switches one four times.  The following family switches one vertex
$K$ times for every $K$, at an additive cost of $O(1)$ vertices per
reversal, and it is self-dual, so by \Cref{bsr:prop-selfdual} the same count
is attained by the one-sided rule $\mathrm{MR}$.

\begin{definition}[The self-dual leapfrog $\mathrm{SD}(K)$]\label{rbr:def-sd}
Fix $K\ge2$ and put $\eta:=2^{-(K+2)}$,
\[
 \gamma_j:=(-1)^{j+1}2^{\,j+1}\eta\ (1\le j\le K-1),\quad \gamma_K:=0,
 \qquad
 \Delta:=-\eta-\sum_{j=1}^{K}\gamma_j\bigl(1-2^{-j}\bigr),
\]
$\alpha_j:=\max(\gamma_j,0)$, $\beta_j:=\max(-\gamma_j,0)$,
$S:=\sum_j(\alpha_j+\beta_j)$, $a_p:=\tfrac12(1-S+\Delta)$,
$a_q:=\tfrac12(1-S-\Delta)$ (both are nonnegative dyadic rationals).
$\mathrm{SD}(K)$ has
\[
\begin{array}{ll}
 k_j=\mathrm{avg}(t_1,k_{j-1}),\ k_0:=t_0 &(\text{value }1-2^{-j}),\\
 h_j=\mathrm{avg}(t_0,h_{j-1}),\ h_0:=t_1 &(\text{value }2^{-j}),\\
 x_j\in\Vmax,\ x_j\to(x_{j-1},k_j),\ x_0:=t_1, &
 u_j\in\Vmin,\ u_j\to(u_{j-1},h_j),\ u_0:=t_0,
\end{array}
\]
for $1\le j\le K$, together with two average \emph{mixtures}
\[
 p:\ \{x_j\mapsto\alpha_j,\ u_j\mapsto\beta_j,\ t_1\mapsto a_p,\ t_0\mapsto a_q\},
 \qquad
 q:\ \{x_j\mapsto\beta_j,\ u_j\mapsto\alpha_j,\ t_1\mapsto a_q,\ t_0\mapsto a_p\},
\]
realised as binary trees of average vertices, and
$v\in\Vmax$, $v\to(p,q)$, $v'\in\Vmin$, $v'\to(q,p)$.  Start from
$\sigma_0(x_j)=k_j$, $\sigma_0(v)=p$, $\tau_0(u_j)=h_j$, $\tau_0(v')=q$.
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}[$K$ reversals at one vertex]\label{rbr:prop-sd}
$\mathrm{SD}(K)$ is an acyclic, hence stopping, SSG on
$N=K^{2}+5K+10$ vertices (the two mixture trees dominate the count) with
$|\Vmax|=|\Vmin|=K+1$; the map $\varphi$ with
$\varphi(x_j)=u_j$, $\varphi(k_j)=h_j$, $\varphi(p)=q$, $\varphi(v)=v'$,
$\varphi(t_0)=t_1$ (extended to the two mixture trees by their mirror
correspondence) satisfies the hypotheses of \Cref{bsr:prop-selfdual}, and
$(\sigma_0,\tau_0)$ is a mirrored pair.  From $(\sigma_0,\tau_0)$ both
variants of \Cref{def:bsi}, the one-sided rule $\mathrm{MR}$, the rule
$R_{\mathrm{BR}}$ and all-switches take exactly $K$ rounds; at round $t$
$(0\le t<K)$
\[
  C_{\max}=\{x_{t+1},v\},\qquad C_{\min}=\{u_{t+1},v'\},
\]
so $v$ and $v'$ are each switched $K$ times, every $x_j$ and $u_j$ once, and
$M=\max(\val^\tau-\val_\sigma)$ takes the $K+1$ values $2^{-1},\dots,2^{-K},0$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Acyclicity is immediate from the definition, so the only trap is empty and
$G$ is stopping (\Cref{lem:trapchar}).  That $\varphi$ is an involution
with $\varphi(\Vmax)=\Vmin$, $\varphi(t_0)=t_1$ and
$\{\varphi(x^{(0)}),\varphi(x^{(1)})\}=\{\varphi(x)^{(0)},\varphi(x)^{(1)}\}$
for every non-sink is a direct check on the six shapes; the two mixture
trees correspond because $q$'s distribution is the $\varphi$-image of $p$'s
and the tree is built by the same deterministic halving, so
$\varphi(p)=q$.  \Cref{bsr:prop-selfdual} therefore gives
$U=\val^{\tau}=1-L\circ\varphi$ at every round from the mirrored start, and
in particular
\[
  U(p)-U(q)=\bigl(1-L(q)\bigr)-\bigl(1-L(p)\bigr)=L(p)-L(q):
\]
\emph{the guide and the value agree at $v$}, so the veto at $v$ is passed
in both variants exactly when $v$ is improving.

Since the Min part $u_1,\dots,u_K$ reaches $t_0$ through
$u_1\to u_0=t_0$, Min's optimal play in $\val_\sigma$ gives
$L(u_j)=\min(L(u_{j-1}),2^{-j})=0$ for all $j$ and every $\sigma$; dually
$U(x_j)=\max(U(x_{j-1}),1-2^{-j})=1$ for all $j$ and every $\tau$.  Write
$L_t$ for the value at the state in which $x_1,\dots,x_t$ point at their
$x$-successor and $x_{t+1},\dots,x_K$ at their $k$-successor; then
$L_t(x_j)=1$ for $j\le t$ and $=1-2^{-j}$ for $j>t$, so $x_j$ is strictly
switchable at $\sigma_t$ iff $j=t+1$, and its veto reads
$U(x_t)=1>1-2^{-(t+1)}$: $S_\sigma\cap\{x_1,\dots,x_K\}=\{x_{t+1}\}\subseteq
C_{\max}$.  Finally, with $L(u_j)=0$,
\[
 L_t(p)-L_t(q)=\sum_{j=1}^{K}\gamma_jL_t(x_j)+\bigl(a_p-a_q\bigr)
  =\Delta+\sum_{j\le t}\gamma_j+\sum_{j>t}\gamma_j\bigl(1-2^{-j}\bigr),
\]
whose successive differences are $\gamma_{t}2^{-t}=(-1)^{t+1}2\eta$; with
the stated $\Delta$ this telescopes to
$L_t(p)-L_t(q)=(-1)^{t+1}\eta$ for $0\le t\le K-1$ and
$L_K(p)-L_K(q)=(-1)^{K}\eta$.  Hence at each round $t<K$ the vertex $v$,
which points at $p$ when $t$ is even and at $q$ when $t$ is odd, is strictly
switchable and (by the display above) passes both vetoes, and at $t=K$ it is
not switchable.  The Min side is the $\varphi$-image.  Verified in exact
arithmetic for $K=2,\dots,20$: self-duality, the mirror identity
$U=1-L\circ\varphi$ at every round, stopping, the round count $K$, the
switch multiset, the level sequence, and $\val_\sigma=\val^\tau=w^\ast$ at
the halt.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[What $\mathrm{SD}(K)$ settles, and what it does not]\label{rbr:rem-sd}
The largest number of switches at one vertex recorded anywhere before was
$4$ (round $14$'s $Q_{16}$, $258$ vertices).  $\mathrm{SD}(K)$ makes it
unbounded at an \emph{additive} cost of $O(1)$ vertices per reversal.  Each
reversal does consume one fresh $x_j$ and one fresh $u_j$, so a lemma of the
form ``each reversal at $v$ needs a fresh vertex that switches alone, and
such a vertex is spent'' is not refuted here; but such a lemma is not an
obstruction either, since it bounds the switches at $v$ only by the total
number of switches, which is exactly the quantity a superpolynomial family
has to make superpolynomial.  A $K$-fold leapfrog is therefore \emph{not}
the obstruction; recycling the drivers is.  In the notation of
\Cref{rbr:thm-track}, $\mathrm{SD}(K)$ has $A=B=K$ and
$\sum_t|C_{\max,t}|=2K=m+K-1$, so the first display of that theorem is
tight up to $1$.
\end{remark}

\begin{proposition}[Anatomy of $Q_{16}$]\label{rbr:prop-q16}
On the round-$14$ instance $Q_{16}$ and from its printed start, the four
reversals of the Min vertex $c_{10}$ split as follows.  At rounds
$t=0,1,2$ the two actions of $c_{10}$ have \emph{equal} $\val_\sigma$-value,
namely $0$, so the veto $L(\bar\tau(c_{10}))\le L(\tau(c_{10}))$ holds by a
tie and the strict variant refuses the switch; only the fourth reversal, at
$t=3$, has $L(a_0)=\tfrac{6307113667906557856}{40916452043962854245417}
<L(a_1)=\tfrac{397981020654592949762017}{1340750300576574807913824256}$ and
is endorsed strictly.  The reversals of the $U$-order at $c_{10}$ are

(round $1$) and $c_{11}$ (round $2$).  Consistently, the strict variant from

\end{proposition}

\subsubsection{The rate of decay of $M$}

\begin{proposition}[The gain at a maximum-deficit vertex can be an
exponentially small fraction of $M$]\label{rbr:prop-gain}
For $s\ge1$ let $\mathrm{GAIN}(s)$ be the SSG on $s+5$ vertices with
$\Vmin=\{u\}$, $\Vmax=\{z\}$, $\Vavg=\{H,r_1,\dots,r_s\}$ and
\[
 H\to(t_0,t_1),\quad u\to(t_0,H),\quad r_1\to(u,H),\quad
 r_i\to(u,r_{i-1})\ (2\le i\le s),\quad z\to(t_0,r_s),
\]
started from $\sigma(z)=t_0$, $\tau(u)=H$.  It is stopping (it is acyclic),
and
\[
 L=\val_\sigma:\ L(u)=0,\ L(r_i)=2^{-i-1},\ L(z)=0;\qquad
 U=\val^\tau:\ U(u)=U(r_i)=\tfrac12,\ U(z)=\tfrac12 .
\]
Hence $M=\max(U-L)=\tfrac12$, $Z=\operatorname{argmax}(U-L)$ contains $z$,
and $z$ lies in $C_{\max}$ in both variants with
\[
 \val_\sigma(\bar\sigma(z))-\val_\sigma(\sigma(z))\;=\;2^{-s-1}\;=\;M\cdot2^{-s}
 \;=\;M\cdot2^{-(N-5)} .
\]
So the assertion ``the switched $Z$-vertex's gain is at least a constant
fraction of $M$'' is false, and false by an exponential factor.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
$L(r_i)=\tfrac12(L(u)+L(r_{i-1}))$ with $L(r_0):=L(H)=\tfrac12$ and
$L(u)=\min(0,\tfrac12)=0$ gives $L(r_i)=2^{-i-1}$;
$U(r_i)=\tfrac12(U(u)+U(r_{i-1}))$ with $U(u)=U(H)=\tfrac12$ gives
$U(r_i)=\tfrac12$.  Then $U(z)-L(z)=\tfrac12=M$ and
$U(r_s)=\tfrac12\ge U(t_0)=0$, so $z\in C_{\max}$ with gain
$L(r_s)-L(t_0)=2^{-s-1}$.  Verified exactly for
$s=1,2,4,8,12,16,20,24,30,40$.  The general identity behind the example is
$M=\mathrm{gain}+\bigl(U(q)-L(q)\bigr)$ at a switched
$z\in Z\cap C_{\max}$ with target $q$: the gain is small exactly when the
target is itself almost of maximal deficit, and the chain $r_1,\dots,r_s$
makes the deficit of the target approach $M$ geometrically.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[$M$ can fall by a $2^{-\Theta(N)}$ fraction per
level]\label{rbr:prop-slowlevel}
For $K\ge2$ let $\mathrm{SL}(K)$ be the self-dual stopping SSG on
$N=6K+4$ vertices with chains $h_i$ of value $2^{-i}$ and $g_i$ of value
$1-2^{-i}$, gadgets $e_i=\mathrm{avg}(t_1,h_i)$ of value
$c_i:=\tfrac12+2^{-i-1}$ and $f_i=\mathrm{avg}(t_0,g_i)$ of value $1-c_i$, and
\[
  u_i\in\Vmin,\ u_i\to(u_{i-1},e_i),\ u_0:=t_0;\qquad
  x_i\in\Vmax,\ x_i\to(x_{i-1},f_i),\ x_0:=t_1 ,
\]
started at $\tau_0(u_i)=e_i$, $\sigma_0(x_i)=f_i$.  Then \Cref{def:bsi}
takes $K$ rounds, one $u_i$ and one $x_i$ per round, and
\[
  M_t=\tfrac12+2^{-t-2}\quad(0\le t\le K-1),\qquad M_K=0 .
\]
So $M$ stays above $\tfrac12$ for all $K=\Theta(N)$ rounds and its relative
drop at round $t$ is $2^{-t-3}/(\tfrac12+2^{-t-2})$, which is
$2^{-\Theta(N)}$ at the late rounds.  Hence no per-round or per-level
geometric decay of $M$ holds.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
$c_1>c_2>\dots>c_K>\tfrac12$, so $U(u_{i-1})=c_{i-1}>c_i$ for $i\ge2$ and
only $u_1$ is in $S^{\tau_0}$; the veto reads $L(u_{i-1})=0\le c_i$ and
holds.  After $t$ rounds $U(u_i)=0$ for $i\le t$ and $=c_i$ for $i>t$, and
$L(u_i)=0$ throughout, so the deficit at $u_i$ is $c_i$ before its round and
$0$ after; the Max side is the $\varphi$-image and contributes the same
deficits.  Every other vertex is average with $L=U$.  Hence
$M_t=\max_{i>t}c_i=c_{t+1}$.  Verified exactly for
$K=2,3,4,6,8,10,12,16$, together with $\val_\sigma=\val^\tau=w^\ast$ at
the halt.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}\label{rbr:rem-rate}
\Cref{rbr:prop-gain,rbr:prop-slowlevel} close the local half of the rate
question: neither ``the gain at the switched $Z$-vertex is a constant
fraction of $M$'' nor ``$M$ falls by a constant factor at each level'' is
available, and both fail by $2^{-\Theta(N)}$.  What is \emph{not} settled,
and cannot be settled by an instance, is the global statement ``$M$ is
halved every $\mathrm{poly}(N)$ rounds'': in $\mathrm{SL}(K)$ the number of
levels is $K=\Theta(N)$, so $M$ is halved within $O(N)$ rounds after all.
By \Cref{cor:bsi-levels} the global statement is equivalent to a polynomial
bound on the number of levels, which is the target.
\end{remark}

\subsubsection{Best-response restart is not faster than all-switches}

\Cref{rem:bsi-br} records that on every instance measured there,
$R_{\mathrm{BR}}$ was at least as fast as all-switches --- $\lfloor\log_2
n\rfloor+1$ against $n$ on $L_n$, $4$ against $7$ on $G^{\sharp}$.  It is
not, and the discrepancy is unbounded.

\begin{definition}[The readout cascade $\mathrm{RD}(n)$]\label{rbr:def-rd}
Let $f(x):=\tfrac{x}{2}+\tfrac14$ (fixed point $\tfrac12$) and, for
$1\le j\le n$,
\[
  \theta_j:=\tfrac12-4^{-j},\qquad B_j:=\tfrac12+4^{-j},
\]
so that $f(\theta_j)<\theta_{j+1}<B_{j+1}<f(B_j)$ and $\theta_j<B_j$.
$\mathrm{RD}(n)$ has $H=\mathrm{avg}(t_0,t_1)$, average gadgets $\Theta_j$
of value $\theta_j$ and $b_j$ of value $B_j$ (dyadic chains of $O(1)$
vertices each, sharing two chains of length $2n$), and
\[
 a_1:=t_0,\qquad a_j:=\mathrm{avg}(u_{j-1},H)\ (j\ge2),\qquad
 v_j\in\Vmax,\ v_j\to(a_j,b_j),\qquad u_j\in\Vmin,\ u_j\to(v_j,\Theta_j),
\]
so that $\val(a_j)=f(\val(u_{j-1}))$.  Start from $\sigma_0(v_j)=a_j$ and
(for \Cref{def:bsi}) $\tau_0(u_j)=v_j$.  $\mathrm{RD}(n)$ is acyclic, hence
stopping, and has $N=9n$ vertices, $|\Vmax|=|\Vmin|=n$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[All-switches one round, $R_{\mathrm{BR}}$ $n$ rounds, BSI
$2n$ rounds]\label{rbr:thm-readout}
On $\mathrm{RD}(n)$:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
\item all-switches halts after at most $1$ round from \emph{every} Max
      strategy (and after exactly $1$ from $\sigma_0$);
\item from $\sigma_0$, $R_{\mathrm{BR}}$ of \Cref{prop:bsi-br} takes
      exactly $n$ rounds, in both veto variants and for every choice of best
      response, switching the single vertex $v_{t+1}$ at round $t$ (the worst
      case over all $2^{n}$ Max starts is again $n$, verified for $n\le4$);
\item \Cref{def:bsi} from $(\sigma_0,\tau_0)$ takes exactly $2n$ rounds,
      alternating $C_{\max}=\{v_{t+1}\},C_{\min}=\emptyset$ and
      $C_{\max}=\emptyset,C_{\min}=\{u_{t+1}\}$, in both variants (the worst
      case over all $4^{n}$ pair starts is again $2n$, verified for $n\le3$);
\end{enumerate}
every controlled vertex is switched once, and every run halts at
$\val_\sigma=\val^\tau=w^\ast$.  Hence the ratio of the round count of
either rule to that of all-switches is $\Theta(N)$ and unbounded.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Let $\sigma_t$ be the strategy with $\sigma_t(v_j)=b_j$ for $j\le t$ and
$a_j$ for $j>t$, and $L_t:=\val_{\sigma_t}$.  Min plays optimally in
$L_t$, so $L_t(u_j)=\min(L_t(v_j),\theta_j)$.  We show by induction that
\begin{equation}\label{rbr:eq-Lt}
  L_t(v_j)=B_j\ (j\le t),\qquad L_t(u_j)=\theta_j\ (j\le t),\qquad
  L_t(v_j)<\theta_j\ (j>t).
\end{equation}
For $j\le t$, $L_t(v_j)=B_j>\theta_j$ gives $L_t(u_j)=\theta_j$.  For
$j=t+1$, $L_t(v_{t+1})=L_t(a_{t+1})=f(L_t(u_t))=f(\theta_t)<\theta_{t+1}$
(and $L_0(v_1)=L(t_0)=0<\theta_1$); for $j>t+1$,
$L_t(u_{j-1})=L_t(v_{j-1})<\theta_{j-1}$ so
$L_t(v_j)=L_t(a_j)=f(L_t(u_{j-1}))<f(\theta_{j-1})<\theta_j$.
Thus at $\sigma_t$ every $v_j$ with $j>t$ is strictly switchable
($L_t(v_j)<\theta_j<B_j$) and none with $j\le t$ is
($L_t(a_j)=f(\theta_{j-1})<B_j$, and $L_t(a_1)=0<B_1$).  In particular
$S_{\sigma_0}=\{v_1,\dots,v_n\}$ and $S_{\sigma_n}=\emptyset$, which is (a)
from $\sigma_0$ by \Cref{lem:local-global}.  For (a) from an arbitrary
$\sigma$ the same computation applies verbatim: $L(u_j)\le\theta_j$ always,
so $L(a_j)=f(L(u_{j-1}))\le f(\theta_{j-1})<B_j$ at every $j$ and every
$\sigma$, whence $S_\sigma=\{v_j:\sigma(v_j)=a_j\}$ and one all-switches
round lands at $\sigma_n$, which is optimal.

For (b), \eqref{rbr:eq-Lt} shows that the best response to $\sigma_t$ is
unique and is $\tau_t(u_j)=\Theta_j$ for $j\le t$, $=v_j$ for $j>t$: the
strategy $\tau_t$ \emph{reads off} which Max vertices have switched.  Put
$U_t:=\val^{\tau_t}$.  Then $U_t(u_j)=\theta_j$ for $j\le t$, and for $j>t$,
$U_t(u_j)=U_t(v_j)=\max(f(U_t(u_{j-1})),B_j)$.  Hence
\[
  U_t(a_{t+1})=f(\theta_t)<B_{t+1},\qquad U_t(v_{t+1})=B_{t+1},
\]
so $v_{t+1}$ passes both vetoes; and $U_t(a_{t+2})=f(B_{t+1})>B_{t+2}$, so
$U_t(v_{t+2})=f(B_{t+1})$ and, inductively, $U_t(a_j)>B_j$ for every
$j>t+1$, so every such $v_j$ is vetoed.  Therefore
$R_{\mathrm{BR}}(\sigma_t)=\sigma_{t+1}$ and (b) follows.

For (c), the pair state after $2t$ rounds is $(\sigma_t,\tau_t)$, so the
computation for (b) gives $C_{\max}=\{v_{t+1}\}$; and $C_{\min}=\emptyset$
there, because $u_j\in S^{\tau_t}$ exactly for $j>t$ while its veto reads
$\theta_j=L_t(\Theta_j)\le L_t(v_j)$, which fails by \eqref{rbr:eq-Lt}.
After that Max round the state is $(\sigma_{t+1},\tau_t)$: now
$L_{t+1}(v_{t+1})=B_{t+1}>\theta_{t+1}$, so $u_{t+1}$ passes its veto, while
every $v_j$ with $j>t+1$ is still vetoed by the unchanged $U_t$; hence
$C_{\max}=\emptyset$ and $C_{\min}=\{u_{t+1}\}$, and the state becomes
$(\sigma_{t+1},\tau_{t+1})$.  Verified in exact arithmetic for
$n=2,\dots,20$, including the bracket $\val_\sigma\le w^\ast\le\val^\tau$ at
every round, the worst case over all $2^{n}$ Max starts for $n\le4$, and the
worst case over every choice of best response at every round for $n\le4$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}\label{rbr:rem-readout}
Three consequences.  (i) The veto of \Cref{def:bsi} is not an accelerator:
$\mathrm{RD}(n)$ is a family on which it costs a factor $\Theta(N)$ against
all-switches, so the guide $\val^\tau$ can be as adversarial as one likes
--- which is what a superpolynomial family would need it to be, and is the
first family in this document where it is.  (ii) It removes the last
positive evidence for $R_{\mathrm{BR}}$: \Cref{rem:bsi-br}'s measurements
($L_n$, $G^{\sharp}$) were an artefact of instances whose all-switches runs
are already short relative to $\Vmax$.  (iii) $\mathrm{RD}(n)$ has
$2n$ BSI rounds with $2n$ controlled vertices, so it also raises the largest
BSI round count known here from $11$ (round $14$'s annealing) to $\Theta(N)$.
What it does \emph{not} do is exceed $|C|$: every controlled vertex switches
once.  Combining it with \Cref{rbr:prop-sd} --- whose observer switches at
every round --- is the obvious next construction, and a counter would need
the readout comparisons $\val_\sigma(v_j)$ against $\theta_j$ to reverse,
which by \Cref{rbr:prop-sd} costs one fresh driver per reversal unless the
drivers themselves recur.
\end{remark}

\begin{proposition}[Small instances]\label{rbr:prop-small}
On the stopping SSG with $9$ non-sinks ($t_0=9$, $t_1=10$), types

and successor pairs
$(1,5),(7,9),(2,6),(1,10),(3,9),(1,10),(4,3),(4,0),(2,4)$, from

On the stopping SSG with $10$ non-sinks, types

and pairs $(1,6),(4,0),(10,9),(10,0),(8,9),(0,11),(10,1),(0,5),(2,5),(6,7)$,

\subsubsection{A subclass on which BSI is exactly all-switches}

\begin{definition}[Mirror-paired self-dual]\label{rbr:def-psd}
A self-dual stopping SSG in the sense of \Cref{bsr:prop-selfdual}, with
involution $\varphi$, is \emph{mirror-paired} if $\varphi$ exchanges the two
successors of every controlled vertex: $\varphi(v^{(0)})=v^{(1)}$.  Then
$\varphi(v)$ is a controlled vertex of the opposite kind over the same pair,
so the controlled vertices come in twins $(v_i,v_i')$ over a
$\varphi$-swapped pair $(p_i,q_i=\varphi(p_i))$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[The veto is vacuous]\label{rbr:lem-vacuous}
Let $G$ be mirror-paired self-dual and $(\sigma,\varphi(\sigma))$ a mirrored
pair state.  Then $C_{\max}=S_\sigma$ and $C_{\min}=\varphi(S_\sigma)$, in
both variants, and the next pair state is again mirrored.  Consequently
\Cref{def:bsi}, its strict variant and the rule $\mathrm{MR}$ of
\Cref{bsr:prop-selfdual} all run \emph{exactly all-switches} on the Max
cube of $G$, and their round count is the all-switches round count.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
By \Cref{bsr:prop-selfdual}, $U=1-L\circ\varphi$.  Let $v\in\Vmax$,
$p=\sigma(v)$, $q=\bar\sigma(v)$; mirror-pairing gives $\varphi(p)=q$ and
$\varphi(q)=p$, so
$U(q)-U(p)=(1-L(\varphi q))-(1-L(\varphi p))=L(q)-L(p)$.  Hence $v\in
S_\sigma$ iff $U(q)>U(p)$, which is the strict veto, a fortiori the veto.
So $C_{\max}=S_\sigma$; $C_{\min}=\varphi(C_{\max})$ by
\Cref{bsr:prop-selfdual}, and $\tau[C_{\min}]=\varphi(\sigma[C_{\max}])$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[What the subclass realises]\label{rbr:rem-psd}
\Cref{rbr:lem-vacuous} says that any polynomial round bound for
\Cref{def:bsi} entails one for all-switches on the mirror-paired self-dual
class, so a barrier for BSI would have to explain why that class is easy.
Collapsing the average part (the harmonic normal form of item (v4)) puts the
class in bijection with triples $(A_i,B_i,c_i)_{i\le m}$ of nonnegative
rows with $|A_i|+|B_i|<1$ and $0\le c_i\le1-|A_i|-|B_i|$: $p_i$ is the row
$(A_i\ \text{on}\ v,\ B_i\ \text{on}\ v',\ c_i\ \text{on}\ t_1)$ and $q_i$
is forced to be $(B_i,A_i,1-|A_i|-|B_i|-c_i)$, with
$L(v_i')=\min(L(p_i),L(q_i))$.  Hours of random restart plus hill climbing

\begin{lemma}[A constant option is never a veto in one
direction]\label{rbr:lem-constant}
Let $(\sigma,\tau)$ be a pair state and $v\in\Vmax$ with
$\sigma(v)=c$, where $\val_\sigma(c)=\val^\tau(c)$ (for instance $c$ is an
average gadget all of whose paths end in sinks).  If $v\in S_\sigma$ then
$v\in C_{\max}$, in both variants of \Cref{def:bsi} and in
$R_{\mathrm{BR}}$.  Dually at $\Vmin$.  Hence at a controlled vertex one of
whose two options is a constant gadget, only the switch \emph{towards} the
constant is ever vetoed.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Write $p:=\bar\sigma(v)$.  Then $U(p)\ge L(p)>L(c)=U(c)$ by
\Cref{cor:comparison} and $v\in S_\sigma$, so the veto
$U(p)\ge U(c)$ holds, and strictly.  Verified on $364$ occurrences of the
hypothesis drawn from random stopping games, with no violation.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[The gap]\label{rbr:rem-gap}
Combining \Cref{rbr:thm-track} with \Cref{cor:bsi-levels}: a superpolynomial
BSI family must have \emph{both} tracks superpolynomially long, and hence
some controlled vertex switched superpolynomially often.
\Cref{rbr:prop-sd} shows the second requirement is met by an
$O(1)$-vertex-per-reversal construction, and \Cref{rbr:thm-readout} shows
that the veto can force one switch per round for $\Theta(N)$ rounds.  What
neither does is \emph{recycle} a driver: in $\mathrm{SD}(K)$ each $x_j$
fires once, and in $\mathrm{RD}(n)$ the threshold $\theta_j$ against which
the readout $u_j$ compares $\val_\sigma(v_j)$ is a constant, so by
\Cref{rbr:lem-constant} and the monotonicity of $\val_\sigma$ the readout
can never revert: once $\val_\sigma(v_j)>\theta_j$ it stays so.  The missing
statement is exactly this:
\begin{quote}
\textbf{GAP.}  There is a family of stopping SSGs on $N=n^{O(1)}$ vertices
with Max vertices $v_1,\dots,v_n$, Min vertices $u_1,\dots,u_n$,
$u_j\to(v_j,\Theta_j)$ and $v_j\to(a_j,b_j)$ with $b_j$ a constant gadget,
in which $\Theta_j$ is driven by $v_1,\dots,v_{j-1}$ and the two
nondecreasing quantities $\val_\sigma(v_j)$ and $\val_\sigma(\Theta_j)$ cross
$2^{\,n-j}$ times along the run of \Cref{def:bsi}.
\end{quote}
Two directional facts say where the difficulty is and is not.  By
\Cref{rbr:lem-constant} the \emph{reset} $b_j\to a_j$ of such a counter is
never vetoed, so only the \emph{set} $a_j\to b_j$ needs the endorsement
machinery of \Cref{rbr:thm-readout}; and a crossing of $\val_\sigma(v_j)$ by
$\val_\sigma(\Theta_j)$ is the leapfrog of \Cref{rbr:prop-sd}, which costs
one driver switch each.  So the counter is not blocked by any local or
order-theoretic obstruction found here; what is missing is a schedule in
which the drivers of the leapfrog at $u_j$ are the recurring lower bits
rather than fresh vertices.  This is the same missing object as the
all-switches one (\Cref{cor:ceiling-general}) only in so far as both need a
superpolynomial improving run that a rule actually follows; by
\Cref{rbr:thm-readout} the two rules are \emph{not} comparable, so neither
reduces to the other.
\end{remark}
